Track 01

How models work

Explain tokens, context, sampling, hallucination, and the model families named in current job posts.

Start this track

How models work1 of 10Core12 min

Lesson 01

A model predicts the next token

Why it matters

Fluency is the product of a probability model. It is not a source of record.

Try it: Tokens and attention

Lesson
01 of 10
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Loop
One token at a time
Evidence
Only what is in reach
Confidence
Not a check

A large language model takes the tokens so far and assigns probabilities to what might come next. It then picks one, adds it, and repeats. The result sounds like a person who knows the topic. The mechanism is still next-token prediction.

That is why a model can write a confident paragraph about a library that does not exist, and why it can also write a correct summary of a page you just pasted in. The second case worked because the evidence was in the context, not because the model 'looked it up' in the world.

What to do with this

  • If the fact must be exact, put the source in the context or call a tool that returns the fact.
  • If you need the same decision tomorrow, save the prompt, the model id, and the output. Do not trust memory of a chat.
  • If the model says it is sure, ignore the claim and check the evidence.

Practice

Ask any model, including a local one, for a specific number you can verify from a file on your machine, and do not give it the file. Record whether it was right. Then paste the relevant line and ask again. Save both outputs in one note.

Check

Why can a fluent answer still be false?

Show the answer

Because the model is continuing likely text. Likelihood is not a citation.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Attention heatmap

Causal attention: a position may look at itself and earlier tokens only. The compute mode runs QKᵀ / √d and softmax on fixed toy vectors, with Wq and Wk as identity. The sketch mode is a hand-drawn pattern, not a trained model.
lessons.01-02:
How models work2 of 10Core10 min

Lesson 02

Tokens are the unit of cost and context

Why it matters

A token is a chunk of text, not a word, and every limit you hit is counted in tokens.

Try it: Cost and latency

Lesson
02 of 10
Time
10 min
Level
Core
Unit
Token, not word
Count with
That model's tokenizer
Average
Not a budget

The model does not read letters one by one, and it does not read dictionary words. A tokenizer splits text into chunks. A chunk might be a word, part of a word, a space, or a piece of punctuation. Code and languages other than English often use more tokens for the same idea.

A rough English average is under one token per word, but you should not budget from that average. Count tokens with the tokenizer for the model you are calling. Billing, rate limits, and the context window all use that count.

What changes the countWhat to watch
Pasting a whole repositoryCost and latency jump, and early instructions get crowded out.
JSON and codeMore tokens than the same meaning in a short sentence.
A long chat that keeps the full historyYou pay to resend the past on every turn unless the API caches it.

Practice

Take a 200-word paragraph and a 40-line code file. If you have a tokenizer or a local runner that reports token counts, record both. If you do not, mark the metric as 'not measured yet' and keep the two files for School 03.

Check

Why is 'about 0.75 words per token' not a budget?

Show the answer

It is an English-prose average, not a count for your model, your language, or your code.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Toy tokenizer

Longest match against a tiny vocabulary, then one character at a time. A shipping model uses its own trained tokenizer. Count with that one before you budget a prompt.
lessons.01-03:
How models work3 of 10Core12 min

Lesson 03

The context window is one shared budget

Why it matters

Instructions, retrieved text, the conversation, and the answer all spend the same token limit.

Try it: Context packing

Lesson
03 of 10
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Shared by
Rules, sources, chat, answer
Overflow
Error or truncation
Long window
Can miss the middle

The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model will consider for one request. Input and output share it. There is no separate hidden notebook where the model keeps your system prompt safe while you paste a book.

What happens when you overflow

  • The call errors, or the provider truncates. Read the error. Do not guess which behavior you have.
  • If something is truncated, the standing rules at the start are a common casualty.
  • Stuffing more files does not make retrieval. It makes a larger, less reliable prompt.

Long context is not the same as attention

A model with a large window can still miss a fact buried in the middle. If the fact matters, retrieve it and place it where the instruction says to look.

Practice

Sketch a budget for a task you care about: a percentage for rules, for source text, for the user message, and for the answer. The four parts must add to 100.

Check

Who shares the context window?

Show the answer

The instructions, the retrieved or pasted sources, the conversation, and the tokens the model still has to write.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Context budget and a cost sketch

Instructions, retrieved text, conversation, and reserved answer tokens share one window. Prices start empty. The example button fills placeholders, not a quote. Read your provider's card.
lessons.01-04:
How models work4 of 10Core10 min

Lesson 04

Temperature is a sampling control

Why it matters

Lower settings repeat likely tokens. Higher settings take more risks. Neither setting checks facts.

Try it: Temperature and top-p

Lesson
04 of 10
Time
10 min
Level
Core
Low temperature
Sticks to likely tokens
High temperature
Lets the tail through
Neither
Checks facts

After the model scores possible next tokens, a sampler chooses one. Temperature reshapes those scores. Low temperature, including zero where the API allows it, sticks to the most likely tokens. Higher temperature lets less likely tokens through.

Related knobs, such as top-p, cut the tail of the distribution before sampling. You do not need the math to use them. You need a rule for which tasks may vary.

TaskSampling
Extract JSON, classify, route, or anything you will scoreLow temperature. You want the same input to land on the same structure.
Draft three headlines for a person to pick fromHigher temperature is reasonable. A person is the judge.
A tool call that must match a schemaLow temperature, then validate. Do not 'get creative' on the arguments.

Temperature does not turn a model into a database, and temperature zero is not a promise of bit-identical output across hardware, batching, or model updates.

Practice

Run one factual extraction twice at low temperature and twice at a high temperature, if you have any model available. If you do not, write the setting you will use for scored tasks and the setting you will refuse to use.

Check

Does a low temperature stop hallucinations?

Show the answer

No. It reduces random variation. A likely-but-wrong token can still be the top choice.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

Temperature and top-p

Eight fixed logits. Temperature divides them before softmax. Top-p keeps the smallest high-probability set that reaches p, then renormalizes. Neither knob checks facts. A temperature of 0.05 stands in for greedy decoding; many APIs treat 0 as argmax.
lessons.01-05:
How models work5 of 10Core11 min

Lesson 05

Hallucination is fluent text without evidence

Why it matters

Catch it with sources, tools, and tests. Do not catch it by asking the model if it is sure.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
05 of 10
Time
11 min
Level
Core
Cause
Likely text, no evidence
Weak check
Asking the model
Strong check
Source, tool, or test

In this course a hallucination is an answer that reads well and is not grounded in a source you can check. The model may invent a citation, a function, a date, or a confident 'yes'.

Checks that work

  • A fixed set of questions with known answers.
  • A citation that points at a passage you can open.
  • A tool for facts that must be calculated or looked up in a system of record.
  • A refusal when the source does not contain the answer.

A check that does not work

Asking 'are you sure?' often produces another fluent paragraph. Confidence language is not a metric. Score the evidence.

Fake citations

A bibliography the model typed is not a citation. A citation names an id in your corpus and a span a person can find.

Practice

Write three questions whose correct answer is 'the sources do not say'. You will use them when you build retrieval.

Check

What do you score instead of the model's confidence?

Show the answer

Whether the answer matches a source, a tool result, or a known test case.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.
lessons.01-06:
How models work6 of 10Core11 min

Lesson 06

System, user, and tool messages do different jobs

Why it matters

Put standing rules in the system message. Put the task in the user message. Put tool results in tool messages.

Try it: Function-call check

Lesson
06 of 10
Time
11 min
Level
Core
System
Standing rules
User
This turn's task
Tool
Handler results

Chat APIs send a list of messages, not one blob. The roles are a contract with the model and with the software around it.

RolePut it hereDo not put it here
System or developerRole, standing rules, output shape, safety limits.The user's private document, or a new question every turn.
UserThe task and the material for this turn.Secrets that belong in an environment variable.
AssistantThe model's previous answer, if you are continuing a thread.Text you want the model to treat as an order from you. That is a user or system message.
ToolThe structured result of a tool the model called.Instructions hidden inside a document. Those are data.

Some providers rename 'system' to 'developer' or split policy from instructions. Read the API you are calling. The job split stays the same: standing rules, this turn's task, and tool results are not the same channel.

Practice

Rewrite a messy prompt you have used into three boxes: standing rules, this turn's task, and data. If a sentence could be data that contains instructions, mark it as data.

Check

Where do tool results belong?

Show the answer

In a tool message, separate from the user's request, so the model can see what the tool returned.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.
lessons.01-07:
How models work7 of 10Core14 min

Lesson 07

Model families you will see in 2026 job posts

Why it matters

Hire and design for a role, then pin an id. A family name is not a version.

Try it: Memory fit

Lesson
07 of 10
Time
14 min
Level
Core
First
Pick a role
Then
Pin an id
Search
A separate model

Posts in 2025 and 2026 rarely ask you to recite a parameter count. They ask which model you would call, how you would swap it, and how you would know the swap worked. Group the catalog by job, then check the vendor's current model card before you depend on a name.

RoleWhat it is forNames you will see
Frontier general modelsHard writing, analysis, long context, tool use.Current flagships from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Pin the model id, not the brand.
Reasoning modelsMath, planning, and multi-step tool use where extra compute before the answer pays off.Models sold as reasoning or thinking models. They are slower and often cost more.
Open-weight modelsLocal use, private data, and fine-tuning.Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, DeepSeek, and other families distributed for download. License terms differ.
Small modelsClassification, extraction, routing, on-device work.Roughly the 1B to 8B class, often quantized.
Embedding and reranker modelsSearch. Not conversation.A separate model from the one that writes the answer.
Coding agentsEdits a repository, runs tests, opens a diff.Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex-style agents, Aider, Continue, Cline, and similar. The agent is the product. The model is a part.

Currency

This table is a map of categories as of October 2026, not a shopping list. Model ids move. Your artifact should name the id you called and the date.

Practice

Pick a task you might actually run. Choose a role from the table and write one sentence on why the neighboring role is the wrong default.

Check

Why do you pin a model id?

Show the answer

Because a family name hides version changes that move quality, cost, and safety.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.
lessons.01-08:
How models work8 of 10Practice11 min

Lesson 08

Choose a reasoning model or a fast chat model

Why it matters

Spend extra compute when the task needs a plan. Do not spend it on extraction you can score cheaply.

Try it: Temperature and top-p

Lesson
08 of 10
Time
11 min
Level
Practice
Try first
A fast model on ten tasks
Reasoning
When the plan is the risk
Keep
The cheaper match

A reasoning model spends more tokens, and often more time, before it returns the answer you see. That helps on planning, difficult code, and problems where a wrong first guess is expensive. It is a poor default for 'pull these four fields out of this invoice' if a smaller, faster model already passes your tests.

A simple rule

  1. Write the task and the price of a wrong answer.
  2. Try a fast model at low temperature on ten examples.
  3. If the failures are format and instruction-following, fix the prompt and the schema.
  4. If the failures are multi-step mistakes, try a reasoning model on the same ten.
  5. Keep the cheaper model where the scores match.

Do not chain a reasoning model behind every button in a product because a demo looked thoughtful. Latency is part of the product. School 09 turns this comparison into a gate.

Practice

Describe two tasks side by side: one that deserves a reasoning model and one that does not. Name the metric that would change your mind.

Check

What should you try before you switch on a slower reasoning model?

Show the answer

A fast model on a fixed set of examples, after the prompt and output shape are clear.

Pictures for this lesson. Maps, traces, and annotated cards.

The citation list in this lesson keeps the page and the fetch date.</p></aside><p>A language model turns the tokens so far into a probability for every token that could come next. Everything a chat product shows you is that loop, plus a sampler, plus a contract about messages. This room builds that picture so later rooms on retrieval, tools, and voice have somewhere to attach.</p><h3>01Executive summary</h3><ul><li>At inference, the model does not “look up an answer.” It scores possible next tokens. A sampler picks one, the token is appended, and the score runs again until a stop condition.</li><li>The 2017 Transformer computes those scores with attention: each position mixes information from other positions using queries, keys, and values, scaled by the square root of the key dimension, then passed through a feed-forward network. Residuals and layer normalization wrap each sub-layer. [cite:1]</li><li>Sampling is a separate choice from the network. Temperature reshapes the distribution. Nucleus (top-p) sampling keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p. OpenAI documents temperature on a 0–2 scale and asks you not to change temperature and top-p together. [cite:2] [cite:4]</li><li>An API adds a message list, an instruction channel, usage counts, and a finish reason. OpenAI’s text-generation guide recommends the Responses API for new text work and warns that the output array is not “the string at index zero.” [cite:3]</li><li>Embeddings are a different product from the hidden states inside the chat model. OpenAI’s embedding guide gives default widths of 1536 and 3072 for two third-generation models and recommends cosine similarity. Do not reuse those vectors as if they were the model’s internal residual stream. [cite:5]</li></ul><aside class="callout note"><h3>Why it matters for the lab engineer</h3><p>Interviewers ask this room in disguise: “what is a token,” “why did the model hallucinate,” “what does temperature do,” “where would you put a knowledge base.” Contact-center work asks the same questions with a caller on the line. If you can draw the path from audio transcript to next token to spoken reply, you can debug a voice bot without blaming “the AI.” The rooms on RAG and MCP assume this picture. They do not replace it.</p></aside><h3>02Architecture</h3><p>Primary path. Numbers match the walk-through in the next sections. The SVG is the phase-0 diagram; Studio may repaint it.</p><p>Diagram: Seven stages: text, tokens, embed plus position, blocks, logits, sample, text</p><ul><li>1–2 are your string and the tokenizer. They are not the neural net.</li><li>3–5 are the network: vectors in, a logit per vocabulary token out.</li><li>6 is the sampler. Temperature lives here, not inside attention.</li><li>7 writes text the user sees. A stop, a tool call, or a length cap can end the loop earlier.</li></ul><h3>Mermaid source for a later redraw</h3><pre><code>flowchart LR

  F -.-> D</code></pre><p>The dotted return is the loop. One forward pass produces one new token (or, on some serving stacks, a small draft). The weights do not change during that loop. Learning happened earlier, on another machine, and is outside this diagram. Whether a given model is dense or a mixture of experts is a model-card fact. Meta’s Llama 4 card, fetched 2026-10-14, describes Scout and Maverick as auto-regressive mixture-of-experts models with early fusion, natively multimodal. Scout is 17 billion activated parameters, 109 billion total, 16 experts. Maverick is 17 billion activated, 400 billion total, 128 experts. [cite:20] [cite:10]</p><h3>03Deep dive</h3><p>Start from the object the API actually returns: a continuation. You sent text, wrapped as messages. You received text, plus metadata. Between those two strings the provider ran a tokenizer, a network whose parameters are fixed for the call, and a sampler. If you remember only one sentence, remember that the network’s immediate output is a vector of scores over the vocabulary, not a paragraph.</p><p>The 2017 Transformer paper is the architecture this lab uses as the foundation, and it is an encoder–decoder built only from attention. The authors dispense with recurrence and convolution. In the configuration they specify, the encoder is a stack of N = 6 identical layers and the decoder is a stack of N = 6 as well. Each encoder layer has two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention, then a position-wise feed-forward network. Around each sub-layer they put a residual connection and layer normalization, written LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). The model dimension they use for that design is d_model = 512, so the residual add is legal. The decoder adds a third sub-layer that attends over the encoder, and it masks the self-attention so position i cannot see future positions. That mask, plus output embeddings offset by one, is what makes the prediction depend only on tokens already known. [cite:1]</p><p>Those numbers (6 layers, width 512) describe the paper’s base layout, not a model you can buy in 2026. Treat them as the diagram’s legend. As of 2026-10-14, OpenAI’s models page lists a 1.05M-token context window and a 128K max output for gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, and gpt-6-luna. That page does not publish layer count or hidden width, so those stay off this diagram. [cite:10] The BLEU scores in the paper — 28.4 on WMT 2014 English-to-German and 41.0 on English-to-French, the big model trained for 3.5 days on eight GPUs — are historical results. They are not a claim about current translation quality. [cite:1]</p><h3>Three places a fact can live</h3><p>When an answer is wrong, the first diagnostic cut is where the fact was supposed to come from. If the fact was absent from both the weights and the context, no temperature will fetch it.</p></aside><aside class="callout note"><h3>Gotcha</h3><p>OpenAI’s chat-completions reference says to alter temperature or top_p, not both. Both knobs reshape the same distribution. Turning them at once makes a regression impossible to read. The documented temperature range on that endpoint is 0 to 2. Higher values such as 0.8 are described as more random; lower values such as 0.2 as more focused. [cite:4] The fetched chat-completions page documents the range 0 to 2. It does not say that 0 is greedy argmax. This room does not claim that it is.</p></aside><h3>Worked example: softmax, then temperature</h3><p>This arithmetic is a teaching example. It is not the output of a product model. Softmax turns logits into probabilities that sum to 1. Subtracting the max logit before the exponential is the stable way to compute it and does not change the result.</p><p>Take three candidate tokens with logits 2, 1, and 0. Subtract 2. The shifted logits are 0, −1, and −2. The exponentials are about 1, 0.3679, and 0.1353. Their sum is about 1.5032. The probabilities are about 0.665, 0.245, and 0.090. The mode holds about two thirds of the mass. The tail is small but not empty.</p><p>A common definition of temperature T is to divide the logits by T before softmax. At T = 0.5 the logits become 4, 2, and 0. Exponentials are about 54.60, 7.389, and 1. The sum is about 62.99. Probabilities are about 0.867, 0.117, and 0.016. The distribution got sharper, which matches the docs’ description of lower temperature as more focused. [cite:4] At T = 2 the same logits become 1, 0.5, and 0. Exponentials are about 2.718, 1.649, and 1. The sum is about 5.367. Probabilities are about 0.507, 0.307, and 0.186. The tail grew. That is the whole mechanism. Nothing in the attention block moved.</p><p>Teaching chart for logits 2, 1, 0. Bar length is probability, not a benchmark.</p><p>Each row shows only the top token’s probability so you can see the mode shrink as temperature rises. The other two tokens take the rest.</p><h3>Worked example: one query, two keys</h3><p>Scaled dot-product attention is the formula in the paper: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K transpose / sqrt(d_k)) V. The scale exists because if the components of a query and a key are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance d_k, and large magnitudes push softmax into a flat-gradient region. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) counters that. [cite:1]</p><p>Teaching numbers, not a trained head. Let d_k = 2 so sqrt(d_k) is about 1.414. One query q = [1, 0]. Two keys: k1 = [1, 0] and k2 = [0, 1]. Dot products are 1 and 0. Scaled scores are about 0.707 and 0. Exponentials are about 2.028 and 1. Softmax weights are about 0.670 and 0.330. If the values are vectors v1 and v2, the output is 0.670 v1 + 0.330 v2. The query mostly copies the value that matched it, and still leaks a third of the other value. Masking, in the decoder, would set a disallowed score to negative infinity before softmax so its weight becomes zero. [cite:1]</p><p>Multi-head attention runs several of these projections and concatenates. The paper uses multi-head attention in three places: encoder self-attention, decoder self-attention with the causal mask, and decoder–encoder attention. [cite:1] A chat model you call may only expose the decoder side of that idea. Neither the OpenAI models page nor the Llama 4 card publishes a Vaswani-style encoder–decoder layer diagram. The Llama 4 card says the models are auto-regressive mixture-of-experts with early fusion. [cite:10] [cite:20]</p><h3>Nucleus sampling, beside temperature</h3><p>Holtzman and co-authors define nucleus (top-p) sampling as drawing from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p. The set grows and shrinks with the shape of the distribution at that step. The point of the paper is to cut an unreliable tail without freezing the candidate count the way a fixed top-k does. [cite:2]</p><p>Apply that definition to the T = 1 example, probabilities 0.665, 0.245, 0.090, already sorted. If p = 0.9, the first token’s mass is 0.665, which is under 0.9. Adding the second reaches about 0.910, which clears 0.9. The nucleus is the first two tokens. The third is discarded, and you renormalize over the two that remain. If p = 0.5, the first token alone already exceeds 0.5, so the nucleus is one token. That is not the same operation as temperature. Temperature rewrote every logit. Nucleus deleted a tail and renormalized.</p><p>OpenAI’s parameter <code>top_p</code> is documented as this idea: the model considers tokens within the top_p probability mass, and 0.1 means the tokens comprising the top 10 percent of mass. [cite:4] Keep the paper’s “smallest set whose cumulative mass exceeds p” and the vendor’s wording next to each other when you implement. If they ever diverge for a model, the vendor’s API reference is what your code must obey, and the paper is what you cite for the idea. [cite:2]</p><h3>What the message API adds</h3><p>The network does not know it is in a “system” role. Stop when you can say the leaf without looking.</p><h3>L0 · What is a language model, in one sentence?</h3><p>A language model assigns a probability to the next token given the tokens so far, and a sampler turns that distribution into the token you append. [cite:1]</p><h3>L1 · Why does next-token prediction exist, and what breaks if you treat the model as a database?</h3><p>The Transformer was built as a sequence transducer: it predicts from context it can attend to, it does not commit to storing a retrievable record with a primary key. If you treat it as a database, updates do not land until you retrain or you put the new fact in the window, and you get no provenance. The RAG paper states both problems directly: manipulating knowledge precisely is limited, and provenance plus updating world knowledge were open problems for parametric models. [cite:7]</p><h3>L2 · How does a string become the next token, end to end?</h3><p>The API renders messages into a string, the tokenizer emits ids, embeddings plus a positional signal enter the stack, each block mixes positions with masked attention and a feed-forward sub-layer, the last projection emits logits, softmax (after temperature or nucleus) yields a distribution, one id is chosen, and the loop repeats until stop. Then ids become text. [cite:1] [cite:3]</p><h3>L2 · Where does word order enter if attention itself has no recurrence?</h3><p>The paper adds positional encodings to the embeddings because the model has no recurrence and no convolution. Sinusoidal encodings and learned positional embeddings scored nearly the same in their experiment. [cite:1] Meta’s Llama 4 blog, fetched 2026-10-14, names iRoPE for that family: RoPE on most layers, interleaved layers without positional embeddings, and inference-time temperature scaling of attention. The OpenAI models page fetched the same day does not name a scheme. [cite:21] [cite:10]</p><h3>L3 · The answer is wrong. How do I prove whether the failure is sampling, attention, or missing knowledge?</h3><p>Collect the rendered prompt, the model id, temperature, top_p, finish reason, and — if you asked — logprobs. If the needed fact is not in the prompt and not something you can defend from the system card’s training description, call it missing knowledge and go to retrieval or a tool. If the fact is in the prompt and logprobs show a close second token, call it sampling and sweep one knob. If the fact is in the prompt, the probability of the bad continuation is high, and a shorter prompt that contains only that fact answers correctly, suspect distraction or instruction priority, not “broken attention,” and test by moving the fact and tightening the instruction. A picture of one attention head is not proof. [cite:4]</p><h3>L3 · What single change separates a sampling bug from a retrieval bug?</h3><p>Put the gold sentence alone in the context and set a focused temperature, leaving top_p at default. If the model now states the sentence, the weights and the sampler can express it, and the earlier failure was the absence or the burial of evidence. If it still invents a different fact, you are looking at instruction-following or a refusal, not at a missing index. [cite:4] [cite:7]</p><h3>L4 · How does this differ across OpenAI, Anthropic, and an open-weight runtime?</h3><p>The computation — ids, a frozen network, a sampler — is the shared idea. The contract differs. OpenAI’s text guide tells you to prefer the Responses API and to treat <code>instructions</code> as higher priority than <code>input</code>. [cite:3] Anthropic’s message and tool schema is taught in T4, not copied here. An open-weight runtime makes the sampler and the chat template your problem. The Llama 4 Community License is the file beside those weights, fetched 2026-10-14. [cite:22] The chat template and the tokenizer merge table live in the generation cookbook, which this pass did not read, This room does not name that template. Do not claim feature parity.</p><h3>L4 · How does the same model sit on a Webex or UCCE call?</h3><p>The phone system still owns the leg: SIP or the CCaaS task, the queue, the recording decision. Speech recognition produces the text that becomes the user message. The model computes the next tokens of a reply or a tool request. Speech synthesis speaks the text. Transfer back to a human is a routing action, not a token. Check the admin guide for the product version on the tenant. Variable names differ by product and release. The computation in this room does not change when the caller is on CUCM.</p><h3>L5 · If I redesigned the decoder, what would I change, and what stops me?</h3><p>I would want a longer reliable use of evidence in the middle of the window, a cheaper way to reuse previous keys and values, and a sampler default that does not surprise an on-call engineer. The constraint is not a slogan about scale. It is whatever the serving stack and the model card actually guarantee: memory for the cache, the trained positional scheme, and the latency budget of a phone call. Check the serving stack for cache bytes; they vary with length, layers, precision, and batch. Check your hop traces for a phone-call millisecond budget; it varies with the edge. The 2017 paper already records the motive for positions that might extrapolate past the trained length, and it also records that learned positions merely matched sinusoids in their test — extrapolation was a hypothesis, not a measured promise for today’s windows. [cite:1]</p><h3>L5 · What would an infinite context window still not give me?</h3><p>Provenance, an update path that does not require rereading the entire corpus into the prompt, and a price I can pay per call. The RAG paper’s reason for a non-parametric index is that you can replace that memory when the world changes. [cite:7] A huge window is still parametric-plus-paste. It does not by itself cite a paragraph or drop a stale one.</p><h3>Leaf · What does temperature multiply or divide?</h3><p>In the definition used in this room, temperature divides the logits before softmax. It does not scale attention weights inside the block. The worked numbers are in the deep dive. The vendor still owns the exact implementation, including temperature 0. [cite:4] The page does not say that 0 is greedy argmax, and this room does not claim that it is.</p><h3>Leaf · Why is cosine the default for retrieval embeddings but not the score inside attention?</h3><p>They are different objects. Attention uses scaled dot products of learned queries and keys, then softmax, as written in the Transformer paper. [cite:1] Retrieval embeddings are compared across documents; OpenAI’s embedding guide recommends cosine similarity for that search. [cite:5] Cosine is not “how attention works.”</p><h3>Leaf · What would I measure before I fine-tune?</h3><p>Whether the failure survives a focused temperature and a prompt that already contains the gold fact. If it does not survive, fine-tuning is the wrong tool. The comparison protocol is T6-R01 and T6-R06. The principle follows from the three places a fact can live, plus the sampler docs. [cite:4]</p><h3>09Lab</h3><p>No API key is required. The point is to compute the objects the room names. Optional steps that need a key are marked and can be skipped.</p><ul><li>Goal: by hand, turn three logits into probabilities at two temperatures, apply a nucleus cutoff, and write five sentences that use only those results.</li><li>Prerequisites: this room’s deep dive. A provider account is optional. No tenant, no Control Hub, no GPU. LlamaIndex’s framework docs say MIT, and pgvector’s LICENSE on master is the PostgreSQL-style grant, both read 2026-10-14. [cite:18] [cite:19]</li><li>Step 1. Logits 2, 1, 0. Compute softmax at T = 1 using the shifted-logit method. Expected: probabilities about 0.665, 0.245, 0.090.</li><li>Step 2. Divide logits by 0.5 and by 2. Recompute. Expected: the top token’s mass rises at 0.5 (about 0.867) and falls at 2 (about 0.507).</li><li>Step 3. On the T = 1 distribution, apply nucleus p = 0.9 and p = 0.5. Expected: two tokens survive at 0.9; one survives at 0.5. Renormalize and write the new probabilities.</li><li>Step 4. Query [1, 0], keys [1, 0] and [0, 1], d_k = 2. Compute scaled scores and softmax weights. Expected: about 0.670 and 0.330.</li><li>Step 5. In one paragraph, state which of those operations lives in the sampler and which lives in the block. Expected: temperature and nucleus in the sampler; scaled dots in the block.</li><li>Evidence: a photo or a notebook page with the four calculations and the paragraph. [cite:4]</li><li>Optional, only if you already have a key: send one short completion with logprobs enabled on an endpoint that documents them, and confirm the response carries a logprob per output token. [cite:4]</li><li>Reflection: what surprised you — the size of the tail at T = 1, or the fact that attention still leaked a third of the unmatched value?</li></ul><h3>10Quiz</h3><p>Multiple choice</p><h3>Q1. The paragraph is a loop of samples, detokenized. The retrieval embedding is a different model. [cite:1]</p><p>Multiple choice</p><h3>Q2. Why does the Transformer paper divide the query–key dot products by the square root of d_k?</h3><ol><li>To convert the score into a probability by itself.</li><li>Because unscaled dots grow in magnitude with d_k and push softmax into a region of tiny gradients.</li><li>To implement nucleus sampling.</li><li>To add word order.</li></ol><h3>Reveal</h3><p>B. [cite:5] [cite:6]</p><p>Scenario</p><h3>Q6. A bot answers a billing question with a confident, specific, and false credit. The policy PDF was never retrieved. <article class="lesson" id="01-p-t1r03" data-panel="lesson" data-school="01" data-title="Transformers and attention, walked through" data-search="01-p-t1r03 transformers and attention, walked through attention is a weighted sum of value vectors. the weights come from scaled dots between a query and the keys. this room walks that formula with numbers, then says what a 2026 model card adds and what it still refuses to draw. note verification source note: last-verified was left unmarked until a person checks the cited pages. the citation list in this lesson keeps the page and the fetch date. p attention is a weighted sum of value vectors. the weights come from scaled dots between a query and the keys. this room walks that formula with numbers, then says what a 2026 model card adds and what it still refuses to draw. h 01executive summary ul vaswani et al. define scaled dot-product attention as softmax of qk transpose, divided by the square root of the key dimension, times v. multi-head attention runs that several times and concatenates. the base model in the paper is 6 layers, d_model 512, 8 heads, d_k 64, and a feed-forward inner width of 2048. those integers are the 2017 experiment, not a product you can call. [cite:1] the decoder uses a causal mask so a position cannot attend to future tokens. the paper also has encoder–decoder attention. a chat model often keeps only the causal decoder stack. confirm that on the card. the llama 4 card says auto-regressive mixture-of-experts with early fusion. it does not publish a vaswani layer diagram. [cite:1] [cite:2] residuals and layer normalization sit around each sublayer in the paper: the sublayer output is added back to its input, then normalized. the feed-forward sublayer is position-wise. it is not the retrieval index. [cite:1] meta’s llama 4 blog names irope: rope on most layers, interleaved layers with no positional embeddings, and inference-time temperature scaling of attention. scout’s card lists a 10 million-token context. the blog says scout was pre-trained and post-trained with a 256k context length, “which empowers the base model with advanced length generalization capability,” and it separately names a supported context of 10 million tokens. keep both. [cite:3] [cite:2] temperature in the sampler divides logits before the next-token softmax. it is a different knob from the attention-temperature scaling the llama 4 blog describes inside the block. do not collapse them. [cite:4] [cite:3] note why it matters for the lab engineer a contact-center demo that “shows attention” is often a heatmap with no claim you can defend. this room is the defense: you can compute one head by hand, you can say what the mask removes, and you can refuse to treat a product screenshot as the 2017 diagram or as a faithful explanation of a sentence. the caller still hears text. the math is how you stop inventing a reason the bot said the wrong credit. h 02architecture p one query, two keys, a scale, a softmax, and a mix of values. teaching numbers, not a vendor diagram. p where attention sits in a decoder block, between the residual stream and the feed-forward sublayer. p diagram: seven stages from token embeddings through masked attention, residual, feed-forward, and logits ul 1–2 are embeddings plus a positional scheme. the 2017 paper adds sinusoids because there is no recurrence. 3 is masked self-attention. future positions are not keys for this token. 4–6 are the residual, the position-wise feed-forward, and the next residual. 7 is the logit vector t1 already taught. p sequence: one new token reuses cached keys and values from earlier positions. p diagram: app, embedder, attention block, feed-forward, sampler, and the cache of past keys and values p the sequence picture is the decode loop. the first token of a reply attends over the prompt. each later token attends over the prompt and the tokens already chosen, under the causal mask. a cache stores keys and values so the server does not recompute them. check the serving stack you run for cache memory. the byte size varies with sequence length, layer count, precision, and batch, which is why a model card does not carry one number. h 03deep dive p start from the sentence the paper actually writes. attention maps a query and a set of key–value pairs to an output. the output is a weighted sum of the values. the weight on a value is the compatibility of the query with that value’s key. scaled dot-product attention computes the compatibility as a dot product, divides by the square root of the key dimension, and applies softmax. the division is there so the dots do not grow with dimension and push softmax into a region with tiny gradients. that is a training motive in the paper. it is also the reason a hand calculation at d_k = 2 looks milder than the raw dots. [cite:1] h one query, two keys, arithmetic you can recompute p let the query be [1, 0]. let the keys be [1, 0] and [0, 1]. the key dimension d_k is 2, so the scale is the square root of 2, about 1.414. the raw dots are 1 and 0. the scaled scores are about 0.707 and 0. softmax of those two numbers is about 0.670 and 0.330. the first key wins, and it does not take all the mass. if the values are [1, 0] and [0, 1], the mixed output is about [0.670, 0.330]. nothing in that paragraph is a vendor guarantee. it is the formula on two vectors you can write on paper. the same pair is the toy on the t1 flashcard. if your calculator disagrees at the second decimal, recompute the exponentials before you “fix” the architecture. table step object this example what it is not ['dot', 'query · key', '1 and 0', 'not cosine. cosine would divide by the norms. openai recommends cosine for embeddings, which is a different comparison. [cite:5]'] ['scale', 'divide by sqrt(d_k)', 'sqrt(2)', 'not temperature. sampler temperature divides logits later. [cite:4]'] ['softmax', 'weights that sum to 1', 'about 0.670 and 0.330', 'not a citation and not an explanation of a sentence.'] ['mix', 'weights times values', 'about [0.670, 0.330]', 'not the token the sampler will pick. that choice is a later softmax over the vocabulary.'] note attention weights are not the reason a product that paints these weights on the words and calls the brightest word “why the model said it” is making a claim this room does not grant. the paper defines a mixing operation. it does not define a faithful explanation. check that product’s own evaluation before you call a map the reason. whether the brightest token explains the output varies by model and by task. h the mask p in the decoder, self-attention is masked so that position i does not attend to positions after i. the paper implements that by setting those future scores to negative infinity before softmax, which drives the corresponding weights to zero. the model can still attend to earlier tokens, including the prompt. it cannot peek at the token it has not produced yet. that is the causal constraint. encoder self-attention in the same paper is not masked that way: every position in the encoder may attend to every other position in the input sequence. chat products that only generate left to right are using the causal idea. they are not required to ship the encoder. [cite:1] p apply the mask to the toy before you celebrate the 0.67. if the second key is a future token, its score becomes negative infinity, its weight becomes zero, and the output collapses to the first value. a demo that forgets the mask will show the model “looking ahead” in a picture that the decoder is not allowed to compute. when you debug a wrong answer, the mask is not the first place to look. the prompt, the tool result, and the sampler are. the mask is the place to look when someone claims the model read a token that had not been generated. h multi-head, residuals, and the feed-forward sublayer p one head is one set of projections. multi-head attention runs h heads, each with its own learned projections of the same input into queries, keys, and values, computes attention in each head, concatenates, and applies a final projection. the paper sets d_k = d_v = d_model / h. in the base model, d_model is 512 and h is 8, so each head has d_k 64. the big model in the paper is larger. quote the row you mean. do not say “transformers have 8 heads” as if that were a 2026 constant. [cite:1] table paper object base model in vaswani et al. how to use the number ['layers n', '6 encoder and 6 decoder', 'historical. llama 4’s card does not publish a layer count of this kind. [cite:2]'] ['d_model', '512', 'the residual width in that experiment. not an embedding-api width. text-embedding-3-small defaults to 1536. [cite:5]'] ['heads h', '8', 'historical. do not copy onto scout or onto gpt-6-astra.'] ['d_ff', '2048', 'inner width of the position-wise feed-forward network in the base model.'] ['wmt bleu', '28.4 english-to-german for the big model', 'a 2014 translation score reported in 2017. not contact-center quality.'] p around each sublayer the paper uses a residual connection and layer normalization. the input to the next sublayer is the normalized sum of the sublayer input and the sublayer output. the residual is why people say the block “adds” attention to the stream instead of replacing the stream. if you remove the residual in a lecture sketch, you have drawn a different network. the feed-forward sublayer is applied to each position separately and identically. it is two linear maps with a relu between them in the paper. it mixes features at one position. it does not mix positions. attention mixed the positions. the feed-forward network does not retrieve a pdf. retrieval is t3. note three mixes, three jobs attention mixes across positions. the feed-forward sublayer mixes across features at one position. the sampler mixes nothing: it picks an id from a distribution over the vocabulary. when a teammate says “the attention hallucinated,” ask which of the three they mean. usually they mean the sampler emitted a token the pack did not support. that bug is faithfulness, taught in t3 and t5, not a broken scale factor. h what llama 4 actually changes in the story p the llama 4 model card, fetched 2026-10-14, describes scout and maverick as auto-regressive language models that are mixture-of-experts, early fusion, and natively multimodal. scout activates 17 billion parameters out of 109 billion total, with 16 experts. maverick activates 17 billion out of 400 billion, with 128 experts. supported languages on the card are arabic, english, french, german, hindi, indonesian, italian, portuguese, spanish, tagalog, thai, and vietnamese. image understanding was tested up to five input images. instruction-tuned checkpoints are for assistant-like chat and visual reasoning. pretrained checkpoints can be adapted for natural-language generation. the card does not name rlhf or dpo. [cite:2] p the blog, fetched the same day, names irope. most layers use rotary position embeddings. some layers are interleaved with no positional embeddings. attention temperature is scaled at inference time. scout was pre-trained and post-trained at a 256 thousand-token context. the blog attaches “advanced length generalization capability” to that sentence. the card’s context-length field for scout is 10 million, which the blog also names as the supported context, and the blog reports results over 10 million tokens of code. maverick’s card lists 1 million. knowledge cutoff on both cards is august 2024. training compute on the card: scout 5.0 million gpu hours, maverick 2.38 million, 7.38 million total, on h100 80 gb accelerators at 700 w tdp. location-based greenhouse gas is 1,999 tons co2eq. market-based is 0 because the card says meta has run net-zero operations since 2020. those figures are the card’s. they are not a serving latency and not a contact-center sla. [cite:3] [cite:2] table fact scout maverick source ['active / total parameters', '17b / 109b, 16 experts', '17b / 400b, 128 experts', 'model card [cite:2]'] ['context length field', '10 million', '1 million', 'model card. blog adds the 256k train length for scout. [cite:3]'] ['tokens in pretraining, about', '40 trillion', '22 trillion', 'model card'] ['knowledge cutoff', 'august 2024', 'august 2024', 'model card'] ['positional scheme', 'irope, as the blog describes it. not printed as a layer diagram on the card.', 'blog [cite:3]', ''] p openai’s models page, fetched 2026-10-14, lists gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.1-sol, and gpt-6-luna at a 1.05 million-token context and a 128 thousand-token max output. it does not publish depth, width, head count, or a positional scheme. you can compare context windows. you cannot compare head counts, because one side did not publish them. behemoth appears in the blog as a previewed teacher, not as a model-card file this room read as a shipped checkpoint. do not quiz a teammate on behemoth’s layer count. [cite:6] [cite:3] h where this sits next to retrieval and tools p attention inside the block reads the tokens that are already in the window. it does not open a database. if the refund policy is not in the prompt, no head will retrieve it. packing a chunk into the window, which t3 teaches, gives attention something to mix. a tool result, which t4 teaches, is more tokens in that same window after the host executes. the host does not run inside a head. mcp revision 2025-11-25 keeps execution in the host. the changelog’s sampling-with-tools change asks the client to sample. it does not move the side effect into q, k, or v. [cite:7] p lost-in-the-middle, liu et al., is a historical claim that models can use information at the start and end of a long context better than information in the middle. the paper is arxiv:2307.03172. it is not a measurement of scout’s 10 million-token window and not a measurement of your contact-center prompt. cite it as a reason to test position, not as a score you can paste onto a bot. [cite:8] h four prompts, the same head p keep the toy head fixed and change only the tokens you imagine in the window. the arithmetic does not become a vendor trace. it becomes a way to talk about four contact-center failures without blaming “attention” for all of them. p prompt a is the policy paragraph at the start and the caller’s sentence at the end: “credits over fifty dollars need a human.” the query at the last position can put weight on “fifty” and on “human.” if the sample then says “i have applied a two hundred dollar credit,” the failure is not that the dot product was undefined. the failure is that a token was chosen which the policy paragraph does not authorize, and that a tool, if one ran, was allowed to commit. attention could have mixed the word “fifty” into the last position and the sampler could still have picked “two hundred.” mixing is not obedience. the fix is the tool cap from t4 and the faithfulness check from t5, not a larger d_k. p prompt b moves the same policy sentence into the middle of a long transcript, with small talk on both sides. liu et al. would tell you to suspect the middle. your job is smaller: copy the sentence to the end, call the model again on a fixture, and see whether the abstention returns. if it returns, you have a position effect on this id, and you still do not have their tables. if it does not return, the model was not using the sentence even when it was adjacent to the query, and rearranging the prompt will not save you. write down which of those two you observed. a story about “lost in the middle” without that swap is a citation wearing a costume. [cite:8] p prompt c is a tool result that arrived after the caller barged in. the text in the window says the assistant already finished a sentence the caller never heard, because nobody truncated. attention will mix that unheard sentence into the next query, because the mask only hides the future, not the past you failed to delete. the repair is t7’s truncate, not a new positional scheme. irope does not know which audio reached the speaker. the blog’s temperature scaling of attention will not drop tokens you left in the prefix. [cite:3] p prompt d is an empty window except the user text “what is the outage in dallas?” no status page was packed. every head, at every width the paper ever used, can only mix the words dallas and outage with whatever the weights already store. the next token may be fluent. it is not a reading of a page you did not provide. this is the same boundary t1-r01 draws among weights, the window, and a tool. attention is the mixer of the window. it is not a fourth place a fact can live. p across the four prompts the head’s formula did not change. the mask did not change. what changed was the set of keys. when you are on call, ask “which keys were in the prefix?” before you ask “is attention broken?” the prefix is the prompt you built, the tool results the host appended, and the tokens the sampler already chose. the projections are the vendor’s, unless you are serving a checkpoint whose license you have read. for llama 4 that license is the community license. for an api model the projections are not yours to edit, and the card may not even list their shapes. [cite:9] [cite:6] p a useful review habit is to separate three sentences you are otherwise tempted to fuse. sentence one: “the 2017 block has residual attention and a position-wise feed-forward network.” sentence two: “llama 4 scout is a mixture-of-experts model with 16 experts and a 10 million context field on the card.” sentence three: “this bot’s last answer contradicted paragraph 4.” only sentence three is an incident. sentence one explains a paper. sentence two explains a card. neither sentence selects a root cause for the credit. people who skip to a heatmap are trying to make sentence one do sentence three’s job. it cannot. p if you teach this room out loud, compute the toy once on a board and then refuse every follow-up that asks for scout’s head count. the refusal is the lesson. the card spent its numbers on experts, active parameters, context, tokens, cutoff, gpu hours, and emissions. it did not spend them on h or d_model. an interviewer who wants eight heads wants the paper. give them the paper, labeled historical, and then give them the card. candidates who can only give one of those two will ship a diagram that matches neither system. [cite:1] [cite:2] p one more distinction belongs in the same breath as the experts. a mixture-of-experts model does not run every expert on every token. the card’s “17 billion activated” against “109 billion total” is the sentence that says so for scout, and the same shape, with 128 experts and 400 billion total, is maverick. the routing that picks experts is not drawn in the card and not drawn in this room. do not invent a router diagram and attribute it to meta. what you can say is that the active count is the compute the card claims per token, and the total count is the parameters that exist. interviewers who add 17 and 109 have misread both numbers. active is not a remainder. [cite:2] p early fusion, the other phrase on that card, means the model is natively multimodal rather than a text model with a vision encoder bolted on in a way the card would have had to describe separately. the card says input can be multilingual text and image, and output is multilingual text and code. it says image understanding was tested with up to five images. it does not say a contact-center screenshot is in domain, and it does not publish a word-error rate for a phone call. bring images into a lab only when the card’s input column includes them, and still evaluate the task you care about. a five-image test on the card is not a five-screenshot warranty for a desktop assist product. [cite:1] h l2 · what does the residual do? p it adds the sublayer output back to the sublayer input before layer normalization, so the block updates the stream instead of replacing it. [cite:1] h l2 · what does the feed-forward sublayer mix? p features at a single position. it does not mix across positions. attention already did that. the base inner width is 2048. A missing source is a refusal.</button></li></ol></figure><div class="prose"><aside class="callout note"><h3>Verification</h3><p>Source note: last-verified was left unmarked until a person checks the cited pages. The citation list in this lesson keeps the page and the fetch date.</p></aside><p>Attention is a weighted sum of value vectors. The weights come from scaled dots between a query and the keys. This room walks that formula with numbers, then says what a 2026 model card adds and what it still refuses to draw.</p><h3>01Executive summary</h3><ul><li>Vaswani et al. define scaled dot-product attention as softmax of QK transpose, divided by the square root of the key dimension, times V. Multi-head attention runs that several times and concatenates. The base model in the paper is 6 layers, d_model 512, 8 heads, d_k 64, and a feed-forward inner width of 2048. Those integers are the 2017 experiment, not a product you can call. [cite:1]</li><li>The decoder uses a causal mask so a position cannot attend to future tokens. The paper also has encoder–decoder attention. A chat model often keeps only the causal decoder stack. Confirm that on the card. The Llama 4 card says auto-regressive mixture-of-experts with early fusion. It does not publish a Vaswani layer diagram. [cite:1] [cite:2]</li><li>Residuals and layer normalization sit around each sublayer in the paper: the sublayer output is added back to its input, then normalized. The feed-forward sublayer is position-wise. It is not the retrieval index. [cite:1]</li><li>Meta’s Llama 4 blog names iRoPE: RoPE on most layers, interleaved layers with no positional embeddings, and inference-time temperature scaling of attention. Scout’s card lists a 10 million-token context. The blog says Scout was pre-trained and post-trained with a 256K context length, “which empowers the base model with advanced length generalization capability,” and it separately names a supported context of 10 million tokens. Keep both. [cite:3] [cite:2]</li><li>Temperature in the sampler divides logits before the next-token softmax. It is a different knob from the attention-temperature scaling the Llama 4 blog describes inside the block. Do not collapse them. [cite:4] [cite:3]</li></ul><aside class="callout note"><h3>Why it matters for the lab engineer</h3><p>A contact-center demo that “shows attention” is often a heatmap with no claim you can defend. This room is the defense: you can compute one head by hand, you can say what the mask removes, and you can refuse to treat a product screenshot as the 2017 diagram or as a faithful explanation of a sentence. The caller still hears text. The math is how you stop inventing a reason the bot said the wrong credit.</p></aside><h3>02Architecture</h3><p>One query, two keys, a scale, a softmax, and a mix of values. Teaching numbers, not a vendor diagram.</p><p>Where attention sits in a decoder block, between the residual stream and the feed-forward sublayer.</p><p>Diagram: Seven stages from token embeddings through masked attention, residual, feed-forward, and logits</p><ul><li>1–2 are embeddings plus a positional scheme. The 2017 paper adds sinusoids because there is no recurrence.</li><li>3 is masked self-attention. Future positions are not keys for this token.</li><li>4–6 are the residual, the position-wise feed-forward, and the next residual. 7 is the logit vector T1 already taught.</li></ul><p>Sequence: one new token reuses cached keys and values from earlier positions.</p><p>Diagram: App, embedder, attention block, feed-forward, sampler, and the cache of past keys and values</p><p>The sequence picture is the decode loop. The first token of a reply attends over the prompt. Each later token attends over the prompt and the tokens already chosen, under the causal mask. A cache stores keys and values so the server does not recompute them. Check the serving stack you run for cache memory. The byte size varies with sequence length, layer count, precision, and batch, which is why a model card does not carry one number.</p><h3>03Deep dive</h3><p>Start from the sentence the paper actually writes. Attention maps a query and a set of key–value pairs to an output. The output is a weighted sum of the values. The weight on a value is the compatibility of the query with that value’s key. Scaled dot-product attention computes the compatibility as a dot product, divides by the square root of the key dimension, and applies softmax. The division is there so the dots do not grow with dimension and push softmax into a region with tiny gradients. That is a training motive in the paper. It is also the reason a hand calculation at d_k = 2 looks milder than the raw dots. [cite:1]</p><h3>One query, two keys, arithmetic you can recompute</h3><p>Let the query be [1, 0]. Let the keys be [1, 0] and [0, 1]. The key dimension d_k is 2, so the scale is the square root of 2, about 1.414. The raw dots are 1 and 0. The scaled scores are about 0.707 and 0. Softmax of those two numbers is about 0.670 and 0.330. The first key wins, and it does not take all the mass. If the values are [1, 0] and [0, 1], the mixed output is about [0.670, 0.330]. Nothing in that paragraph is a vendor guarantee. It is the formula on two vectors you can write on paper. The same pair is the toy on the T1 flashcard. If your calculator disagrees at the second decimal, recompute the exponentials before you “fix” the architecture.</p><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Step</th><th>Object</th><th>This example</th><th>What it is not</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Dot</td><td>query · key</td><td>1 and 0</td><td>Not cosine. Cosine would divide by the norms. OpenAI recommends cosine for embeddings, which is a different comparison. [cite:5]</td></tr><tr><td>Scale</td><td>divide by sqrt(d_k)</td><td>sqrt(2)</td><td>Not temperature. Sampler temperature divides logits later. [cite:4]</td></tr><tr><td>Softmax</td><td>weights that sum to 1</td><td>about 0.670 and 0.330</td><td>Not a citation and not an explanation of a sentence.</td></tr><tr><td>Mix</td><td>weights times values</td><td>about [0.670, 0.330]</td><td>Not the token the sampler will pick. That choice is a later softmax over the vocabulary.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><aside class="callout note"><h3>Attention weights are not the reason</h3><p>A product that paints these weights on the words and calls the brightest word “why the model said it” is making a claim this room does not grant. The paper defines a mixing operation. It does not define a faithful explanation. Check that product’s own evaluation before you call a map the reason. Whether the brightest token explains the output varies by model and by task.</p></aside><h3>The mask</h3><p>In the decoder, self-attention is masked so that position i does not attend to positions after i. The paper implements that by setting those future scores to negative infinity before softmax, which drives the corresponding weights to zero. The model can still attend to earlier tokens, including the prompt. It cannot peek at the token it has not produced yet. That is the causal constraint. Encoder self-attention in the same paper is not masked that way: every position in the encoder may attend to every other position in the input sequence. Chat products that only generate left to right are using the causal idea. They are not required to ship the encoder. [cite:1]</p><p>Apply the mask to the toy before you celebrate the 0.67. If the second key is a future token, its score becomes negative infinity, its weight becomes zero, and the output collapses to the first value. A demo that forgets the mask will show the model “looking ahead” in a picture that the decoder is not allowed to compute. When you debug a wrong answer, the mask is not the first place to look. The prompt, the tool result, and the sampler are. The mask is the place to look when someone claims the model read a token that had not been generated.</p><h3>Multi-head, residuals, and the feed-forward sublayer</h3><p>One head is one set of projections. Multi-head attention runs h heads, each with its own learned projections of the same input into queries, keys, and values, computes attention in each head, concatenates, and applies a final projection. The paper sets d_k = d_v = d_model / h. In the base model, d_model is 512 and h is 8, so each head has d_k 64. The big model in the paper is larger. Quote the row you mean. Do not say “transformers have 8 heads” as if that were a 2026 constant. [cite:1]</p><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Paper object</th><th>Base model in Vaswani et al.</th><th>How to use the number</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Layers N</td><td>6 encoder and 6 decoder</td><td>Historical. Llama 4’s card does not publish a layer count of this kind. [cite:2]</td></tr><tr><td>d_model</td><td>512</td><td>The residual width in that experiment. Not an embedding-API width. text-embedding-3-small defaults to 1536. [cite:5]</td></tr><tr><td>Heads h</td><td>8</td><td>Historical. Do not copy onto Scout or onto gpt-6-astra.</td></tr><tr><td>d_ff</td><td>2048</td><td>Inner width of the position-wise feed-forward network in the base model.</td></tr><tr><td>WMT BLEU</td><td>28.4 English-to-German for the big model</td><td>A 2014 translation score reported in 2017. Not contact-center quality.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>Around each sublayer the paper uses a residual connection and layer normalization. The input to the next sublayer is the normalized sum of the sublayer input and the sublayer output. The residual is why people say the block “adds” attention to the stream instead of replacing the stream. If you remove the residual in a lecture sketch, you have drawn a different network. The feed-forward sublayer is applied to each position separately and identically. It is two linear maps with a ReLU between them in the paper. It mixes features at one position. It does not mix positions. Attention mixed the positions. The feed-forward network does not retrieve a PDF. Retrieval is T3.</p><aside class="callout note"><h3>Three mixes, three jobs</h3><p>Attention mixes across positions. The feed-forward sublayer mixes across features at one position. The sampler mixes nothing: it picks an id from a distribution over the vocabulary. When a teammate says “the attention hallucinated,” ask which of the three they mean. Usually they mean the sampler emitted a token the pack did not support. That bug is faithfulness, taught in T3 and T5, not a broken scale factor.</p></aside><h3>What Llama 4 actually changes in the story</h3><p>The Llama 4 model card, fetched 2026-10-14, describes Scout and Maverick as auto-regressive language models that are mixture-of-experts, early fusion, and natively multimodal. Scout activates 17 billion parameters out of 109 billion total, with 16 experts. Maverick activates 17 billion out of 400 billion, with 128 experts. Supported languages on the card are Arabic, English, French, German, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, Tagalog, Thai, and Vietnamese. Image understanding was tested up to five input images. Instruction-tuned checkpoints are for assistant-like chat and visual reasoning. Pretrained checkpoints can be adapted for natural-language generation. The card does not name RLHF or DPO. [cite:2]</p><p>The blog, fetched the same day, names iRoPE. Most layers use rotary position embeddings. Some layers are interleaved with no positional embeddings. Attention temperature is scaled at inference time. Scout was pre-trained and post-trained at a 256 thousand-token context. The blog attaches “advanced length generalization capability” to that sentence. The card’s context-length field for Scout is 10 million, which the blog also names as the supported context, and the blog reports results over 10 million tokens of code. Maverick’s card lists 1 million. Knowledge cutoff on both cards is August 2024. Training compute on the card: Scout 5.0 million GPU hours, Maverick 2.38 million, 7.38 million total, on H100 80 GB accelerators at 700 W TDP. Location-based greenhouse gas is 1,999 tons CO2eq. Market-based is 0 because the card says Meta has run net-zero operations since 2020. Those figures are the card’s. They are not a serving latency and not a contact-center SLA. [cite:3] [cite:2]</p><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>Fact</th><th>Scout</th><th>Maverick</th><th>Source</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Active / total parameters</td><td>17B / 109B, 16 experts</td><td>17B / 400B, 128 experts</td><td>Model card [cite:2]</td></tr><tr><td>Context length field</td><td>10 million</td><td>1 million</td><td>Model card.
